title: Shalva Wins the Flying City Saubha
story:
While the kings of the earth were still gathered at Indraprastha for the Rajasuya, a man stood up among them and made an oath that turned every head. His name was Shalva, and he was the friend of Shishupala, the king of Chedi whom Krishna had slain at the sacrifice. Shalva had also been at Rukmini's wedding, among the kings who had come to claim her and had gone away defeated: the Yadavas — Krishna's clan — had humbled him once, and now they had killed his friend. In the hearing of all the kings, Shalva vowed that he would make the earth empty of Yadavas.

The kings heard the vow, and some were glad of it, for it is easier to applaud an oath than to keep one. Others shook their heads, remembering how many oaths had been sworn at that sacrifice, and how few had survived the journey home. But Shalva meant his. He left the courts behind and went up into the Himalayas, seeking the lord Shiva, and set himself to win Shiva as his ally.

The penance he undertook was terrible. Day after day, in the cold and silence of the mountains, he ate nothing but a single handful of dust. That was his whole austerity — no fire, no chants, no fasting staged for show — just dust, one handful a day, taken like a man who had forgotten that food belonged to the world he had left behind. The seasons turned above him, and he did not turn with them. Snow came and went on the ridges; the king who had made the vow grew thin, and thinner, until he knelt before his shrine a shadow of himself — and still the handful of dust was his only meal.

Shiva is quickly pleased, and at the end of a year he appeared before Shalva and offered him a boon. Shalva asked for a citadel that nothing could destroy: a city that would move through the sky at its master's will, a fortress that no god, no demon, no man, no spirit of the air, no serpent from the deep, no creature of darkness could overcome or even approach. He had named every power in the three worlds — and set himself above them all. Shiva heard him out and nodded once. A year of dust deserved a straight answer, and the request was granted.

Shiva gave the making of the city to Maya, the master builder whose works had once stood against the gods themselves. At the mountain-lord's command, Maya built Saubha: an iron city, dark as a storm, hard to assail, moving wherever its master willed it. It rose from the mountain into the sky like a piece of night that had decided to travel, and the world looked up at it and felt fear — for a fortress that can move is a fortress that can arrive. The wise called it the abode of darkness, for it sailed wrapped in a gloom of its own, and no weapon of god or demon could touch it.

Shalva climbed into his city. He had his fortress, his weapon, his flying home, and an army gathered beneath its shadow. He stood at the iron ramparts and watched the earth fall away below him, the rivers turning to threads, the mountain ranges to wrinkles. And in the long silences of that flying iron, with the world turning far beneath his feet, his thought went where it had been pointed from the beginning: toward Dwaraka, the sea city of the Yadavas, and the house of Krishna.
reflection: Shalva's vow is the mirror-image of Krishna's silence in the crystal hall: where Krishna waits, Shalva converts grief into a single purpose and gives it a year of his life. The penance buys him power, not wisdom — Shiva grants what is asked, and Shalva asks for war, and the universe politely supplies the weapon.
next_story_tease: In the flying city, Shalva set his course for Dwaraka and the enmity of the Vrishnis.
hero_scene: On a Himalayan ridge, the emaciated king Shalva kneels before the lord Shiva, a single handful of dust raised to his lips, while behind him in the sky the iron city Saubha rises like a piece of traveling night.
